source.name: ASTRA chemistry practice set
source.license: Original syllabus-based practice questions (exam-frequent themes; not verbatim past papers)

questions.stem: The charge carried by one electron is
questions.explanation: The electron is a negatively charged particle of magnitude 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

questions.stem: Cathode rays in a discharge tube led J.J. Thomson to identify the
questions.explanation: Cathode rays are streams of electrons; Thomson measured their charge-to-mass ratio.

questions.stem: Positive rays (canal rays) studied by Goldstein are linked in the textbook with the discovery of the
questions.explanation: Canal rays are positively charged and the lightest such particle is identified as the proton.

questions.stem: James Chadwick established the neutron by bombarding beryllium with
questions.explanation: Be struck by α-particles yields carbon and a penetrating neutral particle, the neutron.

questions.stem: Atomic number Z of an atom equals the number of
questions.explanation: Z is the proton count; in a neutral atom it also equals the electron count.

questions.stem: Mass number A of a nuclide is the total of
questions.explanation: A counts nucleons: protons + neutrons.

questions.stem: Thomson pictured the atom as
options: a tiny positive nucleus with empty space around it
a uniform positive sphere with embedded electrons
electrons moving in fixed circular orbits
questions.explanation: The plum-pudding model spreads positive charge through the atom with electrons embedded in it.

questions.stem: Rutherford inferred that an atom is mostly empty space because
options: every alpha particle bounced straight back
most alpha particles passed through the gold foil undeflected
cathode rays bent in a magnetic field
canal rays had a large e/m value
questions.explanation: Only a few alphas were scattered strongly, so the atom is empty except for a tiny massive nucleus.

questions.stem: The electrical charge on a neutron is
questions.explanation: The neutron is electrically neutral.

questions.stem: Isobars are nuclides that share the same
options: atomic number but different mass number
mass number but different atomic number
questions.explanation: Isobars have equal A but different Z (for example ⁴⁰Ar and ⁴⁰Ca).

questions.stem: Thomson found the specific charge of cathode-ray particles to be
options: independent of the residual gas in the tube
proportional to the atomic mass of the gas
equal to that of the proton
questions.explanation: e/m of cathode rays is the same for all gases, showing they are a common constituent of matter.

questions.stem: Millikan obtained the magnitude of the electronic charge with the
questions.explanation: Charged oil droplets in an electric field gave the elementary charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

questions.stem: The nucleus of an ordinary atom contains
questions.explanation: Nucleons (protons and neutrons) sit in the nucleus; electrons occupy the extra-nuclear region.

questions.stem: A key failure of Rutherford's nuclear model is that it cannot explain
options: the existence of a dense nucleus
why the atom should emit a line spectrum and remain stable
why most of the mass is central
questions.explanation: A classical orbiting electron would radiate continuously and spiral in; a discrete spectrum is also unexplained.

questions.stem: Compared with an electron, a proton has
options: the same mass and opposite charge
nearly 1836 times greater mass and opposite charge
smaller mass and the same charge
questions.explanation: The proton is much heavier and carries charge +e opposite to the electron.

questions.stem: Among electron, proton, neutron and α-particle, the specific charge e/m is largest for the
questions.explanation: The electron has the smallest mass of the charged particles listed, so e/m is greatest.

questions.stem: According to Planck, the energy of one quantum of radiation is
questions.explanation: Planck wrote E = hν, with h Planck's constant and ν the frequency.

questions.stem: Energy of a photon increases when you raise its
questions.explanation: E = hν, so a higher frequency (shorter wavelength) photon is more energetic.

questions.stem: The photoelectric effect is the ejection of electrons from a metal surface by
options: heating the metal in the dark
incident electromagnetic radiation of sufficient frequency
questions.explanation: Photons above the threshold frequency knock electrons out of the metal.

questions.stem: Below the threshold frequency, photoemission from a metal
options: still occurs if the lamp is made extremely bright
does not occur no matter how intense the light
questions.explanation: Each photon must supply at least the work function; intensity cannot replace frequency.

questions.stem: The work function of a metal is the minimum energy needed to
options: ionise a free gaseous atom of that element
just free an electron from the metal surface
promote an electron from n=1 to n=2 in hydrogen
break a metal–metal bond in the bulk crystal
questions.explanation: φ is the binding energy of the least tightly held conduction electron in the metal.

questions.stem: Einstein wrote the photoelectric energy balance as KEmax equal to
questions.explanation: The leftover photon energy after paying the work function appears as kinetic energy of the photoelectron.

questions.stem: Planck's quantum idea and the photoelectric effect together show that radiation has
options: particle character in addition to wave character
rest mass equal to an electron
questions.explanation: Photons explain discrete energy exchange, while interference still requires waves.

questions.stem: A photon of frequency 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz carries energy (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s) closest to
Visible light of wavelength 400 nm carries energy per photon of about (use 1240 eV·nm)
Keeping frequency above threshold, a brighter lamp mainly increases the
options: number of photoelectrons emitted per second
questions.explanation: Intensity raises the photon arrival rate, hence the photocurrent, not KEmax.

questions.stem: If the fastest photoelectrons have kinetic energy 1.8 eV, the stopping potential is
questions.explanation: KEmax = eVs, so Vs in volts equals the kinetic energy in electron-volts.

questions.stem: Light of wavelength 300 nm strikes a surface whose work function is 2.0 eV. Using E(eV) = 1240/λ(nm), the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons is
questions.explanation: Photon energy is 1240/300 = 4.13 eV, so KEmax = 4.13 − 2.0 = 2.13 eV.

questions.stem: Lyman lines of hydrogen arise from jumps that finish at
questions.explanation: The Lyman series is n₂ = 2, 3, 4, … → n₁ = 1.

questions.stem: The Lyman series of hydrogen is observed in the
questions.explanation: Transitions to n = 1 are high-energy and fall in the ultraviolet.

questions.stem: Paschen lines correspond to electron jumps ending at
questions.explanation: Paschen series: n₂ = 4, 5, 6, … → n₁ = 3, in the infrared.

questions.stem: The Brackett series of hydrogen terminates at
questions.explanation: Brackett lines end on n = 4.

questions.stem: Pfund transitions of the hydrogen atom end on the level
questions.explanation: Pfund series: n₂ → n₁ = 5.

questions.stem: Wave number of a hydrogen line is given by Rydberg as
questions.explanation: 1/λ = R(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²) with n₂ > n₁.

questions.stem: A hydrogen discharge tube produces
options: a continuous rainbow with no gaps
questions.explanation: Bound-level jumps give sharp lines rather than a continuum.

questions.stem: An emission line appears when an electron in hydrogen
options: jumps to a higher orbit by absorbing a photon
falls to a lower orbit and a photon is released
stays in the same orbit forever
questions.explanation: The energy difference is carried away as an emitted photon.

questions.stem: Balmer lines are produced when the electron lands on
questions.explanation: Balmer series terminates at n = 2.

questions.stem: The first line of the Lyman series comes from the jump
questions.explanation: The lowest-energy Lyman photon is n = 2 to n = 1.

questions.stem: The hydrogen series found in the infrared and ending at n = 3 is called
questions.explanation: Paschen is the n₁ = 3 infrared series.

questions.stem: The Rydberg constant R has the SI unit
questions.explanation: R is a wave number constant, so its SI unit is m⁻¹.

questions.stem: When an electron drops from n = 4 to the ground state of hydrogen, the number of possible spectral lines is
questions.explanation: From level n the line count is n(n − 1)/2 = 4 × 3/2 = 6.

questions.stem: The longest-wavelength Lyman photon is emitted in the transition
questions.explanation: Among Lyman lines, 2 → 1 has the smallest ΔE and therefore the longest λ.

questions.stem: The series limit of Balmer radiation corresponds to a jump from
questions.explanation: The series limit is ionisation into that series: n = ∞ → n = 2.

questions.stem: For hydrogen, the wave number of the 4 → 2 line equals
Hydrogen atoms excited to n = 5 can emit how many different lines while returning toward n = 1?
questions.explanation: Total lines = 5 × 4/2 = 10.

questions.stem: The red H-alpha line of the Balmer series is the
questions.explanation: Hα is the first Balmer member, n = 3 to n = 2.

questions.stem: Using 1/λ = R(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²) with R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹, the 3 → 2 hydrogen wavelength is closest to
The ratio of wave numbers of the first Lyman line to the first Balmer line of hydrogen is
questions.explanation: First Lyman is 3R/4 and first Balmer is 5R/36; the ratio is (3/4) ÷ (5/36) = 27/5.

questions.stem: Bohr required that a stationary orbit satisfy mvr equal to
questions.explanation: Angular momentum is quantised as mvr = nh/2π, n = 1, 2, 3, …

questions.stem: For hydrogen, Bohr orbit radius grows with n according to
questions.explanation: rₙ = n² a₀, so radius ∝ n².

questions.stem: Total energy of the hydrogen electron in Bohr theory varies as
questions.explanation: Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV, so energy ∝ −1/n².

questions.stem: The lowest Bohr level of hydrogen lies at
questions.explanation: The n = 1 energy is −13.6 eV by definition of the Rydberg for hydrogen.

questions.stem: Bohr assumed that an electron in an allowed orbit
questions.explanation: Stationary orbits are non-radiating by postulate.

questions.stem: A photon is emitted in Bohr's picture when the electron
options: jumps from a higher orbit to a lower one
is at rest at the nucleus
questions.explanation: hν equals the difference of the two stationary-state energies.

questions.stem: The first Bohr radius of hydrogen is about
In hydrogen, the n = 2 Bohr energy is
The energy of hydrogen's third Bohr orbit equals
Speed of the electron in Bohr orbits of hydrogen falls as
questions.explanation: vₙ ∝ Z/n, so for hydrogen v ∝ 1/n.

questions.stem: To strip the electron from ground-state hydrogen you must supply
questions.explanation: Ionisation from n = 1 to n = ∞ requires 13.6 eV.

questions.stem: For a hydrogen-like ion, Eₙ is proportional to
questions.explanation: Eₙ = −13.6 Z²/n² eV.

questions.stem: Bohr radius of a hydrogen-like ion shrinks with atomic number as
questions.explanation: rₙ = n² a₀/Z, so radius ∝ 1/Z.

questions.stem: The hydrogen-like ion He⁺ has nuclear charge number Z equal to
questions.explanation: Helium has two protons, so He⁺ is a one-electron ion with Z = 2.

questions.stem: Bohr's theory does not succeed for
options: a helium atom with two electrons
questions.explanation: The simple Bohr model is for one-electron species; multi-electron atoms need a better treatment.

questions.stem: In a Bohr orbit the kinetic energy of the electron equals
questions.explanation: KE = −E and PE = 2E, so KE = +13.6 Z²/n² eV.

questions.stem: Hydrogen's n = 4 level has energy
The third Bohr orbit of hydrogen is larger than the first by a factor of
questions.explanation: r ∝ n², so r₃/r₁ = 9.

questions.stem: A hydrogen electron falling from n = 2 to n = 1 releases
Angular momentum of the electron in hydrogen's second Bohr orbit is
questions.explanation: L = n h/2π = 2h/2π = h/π.

questions.stem: Ground-state energy of He⁺ is
The n = 1 radius of He⁺ compared with hydrogen's first radius is
questions.explanation: r ∝ 1/Z, so He⁺ (Z = 2) has r₁ = a₀/2.

questions.stem: Ionisation energy of Li²⁺ in its ground state is
The electron speed in hydrogen's first Bohr orbit is about
questions.explanation: v₁ = 2.18 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ (about c/137).

questions.stem: Potential energy of the electron in a Bohr orbit is
questions.explanation: PE = −2 KE, and total E = KE + PE = −KE.

questions.stem: How many times is the n = 4 hydrogen orbit farther from the nucleus than the ground orbit?
questions.explanation: r₄/r₁ = 16 because radius scales as n².

questions.stem: The photon emitted when hydrogen goes from n = 3 to n = 1 has energy
The time period of revolution in Bohr orbits of hydrogen varies as
questions.explanation: T = 2πr/v with r ∝ n² and v ∝ 1/n, so T ∝ n³.

questions.stem: de Broglie related wavelength of a material particle to its mass and speed by
questions.explanation: λ = h/p = h/mv for a non-relativistic particle.

questions.stem: An electron is treated as both particle and wave because
options: it has a rest mass of zero
it shows diffraction as well as charge and mass
questions.explanation: Charge, mass and collisions are particle properties; crystal diffraction is wave behaviour.

questions.stem: Diffraction of electrons from a nickel crystal, shown by Davisson and Germer, proved that
questions.explanation: The observed diffraction pattern matches the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons.

questions.stem: Heisenberg's principle says one cannot simultaneously know, with arbitrary precision, a particle's
questions.explanation: Δx · Δp ≥ h/4π; a sharp position forces a spread in momentum.

questions.stem: A cricket ball has a de Broglie wavelength that is
questions.explanation: Large mv makes λ = h/mv negligible, so matter waves are not seen for everyday objects.

questions.stem: If the momentum of a particle is doubled, its de Broglie wavelength
questions.explanation: λ ∝ 1/p, so doubling p halves λ.

questions.stem: Waves associated with moving material particles are called
questions.explanation: de Broglie matter waves are not electromagnetic; they are associated with the particle's momentum.

questions.stem: An equivalent statement of the uncertainty principle uses the pair
questions.explanation: ΔE · Δt ≥ h/4π is the energy–time form of the uncertainty principle.

questions.stem: de Broglie proposed wave character for
questions.explanation: Any particle with momentum p has wavelength h/p.

questions.stem: At the same speed, a proton's de Broglie wavelength compared with an electron's is
questions.explanation: The proton is far heavier, so at equal v its momentum is larger and λ is smaller.

questions.stem: An electron accelerated through 100 V has de Broglie wavelength about (λ in Å ≈ 12.27/√V)
For an electron given 150 eV of kinetic energy, λ ≈ 12.27/√V Å is nearest to
In Bohr's orbit of quantum number n, the circumference equals
questions.explanation: Standing-wave condition: 2πr = nλ.

questions.stem: If the uncertainty in position of an electron is 10⁻¹⁰ m, the minimum uncertainty in momentum is of order (use h/4π ≈ 5.3 × 10⁻³⁵ J s)
Electrons leaving a 25 V gun have de Broglie wavelength close to
A particle's position is uncertain by 0.1 Å. The minimum Δv for an electron (m ≈ 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, h/4π ≈ 5.3 × 10⁻³⁵) is nearest
questions.explanation: Δx = 10⁻¹¹ m, so Δp ≥ 5.3 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹ and Δv ≥ Δp/m ≈ 5.8 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.

questions.stem: An orbit in Bohr theory is a definite path, whereas an orbital is
options: a region of space with high probability of finding the electron
questions.explanation: Orbitals come from the wave-mechanical probability distribution, not a fixed trajectory.

questions.stem: The quantity |ψ|² at a point gives
options: the probability density of the electron
questions.explanation: |ψ|² dV is the chance of finding the electron in that volume element.

questions.stem: An atomic orbital may be described as
options: a circular wire around the nucleus
the wave-mechanical region where the electron is likely to be
questions.explanation: Each solution of the wave equation (with quantum numbers n, l, mₗ) is an orbital.

questions.stem: Schrödinger's wave equation is the starting point of the
options: quantum mechanical model of the atom
questions.explanation: The quantum mechanical model treats the electron as a wave whose allowed states solve Schrödinger's equation.

questions.stem: The quantum mechanical picture was needed because
options: Bohr orbits could not be reconciled with the wave nature of the electron
questions.explanation: de Broglie waves and uncertainty rule out a thin classical track around the nucleus.

questions.stem: Unlike a Bohr orbit, a 2p orbital
options: has a sharply fixed radius and no angular dependence
has a probability distribution with a nodal plane
questions.explanation: p orbitals have an angular node (a plane of zero probability) through the nucleus.

questions.stem: The wave function ψ itself is
options: equal to the energy in eV
not directly observable, though |ψ|² is physically meaningful
questions.explanation: ψ may be complex; only |ψ|² is the observable probability density.

questions.stem: A node in an orbital is a surface where
options: the probability of finding the electron is zero
the nucleus sits only if Z > 1
questions.explanation: ψ = 0 on a node, so the electron is never found there.

questions.stem: The principal quantum number n primarily indicates
options: size and energy of the shell
questions.explanation: n labels the shell and largely sets the energy and radial size.

questions.stem: For a given n, the azimuthal quantum number l may be
questions.explanation: l runs from 0 up to n − 1.

questions.stem: The magnetic quantum number mₗ runs over
questions.explanation: There are 2l + 1 values of mₗ for a given l.

questions.stem: The spin quantum number of an electron is
questions.explanation: An electron is a spin-1/2 particle, so mₛ = ±1/2.

questions.stem: When n = 1, the only allowed subshell is
questions.explanation: For n = 1, l can only be 0, which is the 1s orbital.

questions.stem: The subshell with l = 2 is labelled
questions.explanation: s, p, d, f correspond to l = 0, 1, 2, 3.

questions.stem: The number of orbitals in a shell of quantum number n is
questions.explanation: Each shell has n² orbitals (and therefore 2n² electrons at most).

questions.stem: Maximum electrons in a subshell of quantum number l equal
questions.explanation: A subshell has 2l + 1 orbitals and two electrons per orbital, so 4l + 2.

questions.stem: The magnetic quantum number mₗ decides
options: the orientation of the orbital in space
questions.explanation: Different mₗ values are the different spatial orientations of a given subshell.

questions.stem: For the L shell (n = 2), allowed l values are
A d subshell (l = 2) contains how many orbitals?
questions.explanation: 2l + 1 = 5 orbitals in a d subshell.

questions.stem: A 4s electron has n and l equal to
questions.explanation: s means l = 0; the leading number is n = 4.

questions.stem: For a 3d electron the pair (n, l) is
questions.explanation: 3d means n = 3 and l = 2.

questions.stem: The letter f stands for l equal to
questions.explanation: f subshells have l = 3 and seven orbitals.

questions.stem: Possible mₗ values for a 2p electron are
questions.explanation: For l = 1, mₗ = −1, 0, +1 (the three p orbitals).

questions.stem: Which set (n, l, mₗ, mₛ) is not allowed?
questions.explanation: l cannot equal n; the maximum l is n − 1, so (3, 3, …) is forbidden.

questions.stem: How many electrons can have n = 3 and l = 1?
questions.explanation: That is the 3p subshell, which holds 4l + 2 = 6 electrons.

questions.stem: The 4d subshell consists of
questions.explanation: Any d subshell (l = 2) has five orbitals.

questions.stem: A valid quantum-number set for a 4d electron is
questions.explanation: 4d requires n = 4 and l = 2, with mₗ between −2 and +2.

questions.stem: How many orbitals belong to the N shell (n = 4)?
questions.explanation: Number of orbitals = n² = 16 (electron capacity would be 32).

questions.stem: Electrons with n = 3, l = 2 and mₛ = +1/2 cannot exceed
questions.explanation: The 3d subshell has five orbitals; each can take one electron of a given spin.

questions.stem: In the n = 4 shell, the number of electrons that can have mₛ = +1/2 is
questions.explanation: There are n² = 16 orbitals, and each may hold one electron of spin +1/2.

questions.stem: The set n = 2, l = 1, mₗ = +2, mₛ = +1/2 is illegal because
questions.explanation: For l = 1 the only mₗ values are −1, 0, +1.

questions.stem: How many electrons in an atom may have n = 4, l = 2 and mₗ = 0?
questions.explanation: Those labels pick out one 4d orbital, which holds two electrons of opposite spin.

questions.stem: The shape of an s orbital is
questions.explanation: s orbitals are spherically symmetric about the nucleus.

questions.stem: A p orbital is typically described as
questions.explanation: Each p orbital has two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus.

questions.stem: Most d orbitals have the appearance of
questions.explanation: Four of the five d orbitals are four-lobed; d_z² is a doughnut-plus-lobes shape.

questions.stem: The pₓ orbital has its lobes along
questions.explanation: The subscript names the axis along which the p orbital points.

questions.stem: The p subshell contains
questions.explanation: pₓ, pᵧ and p_z make three orbitals.

questions.stem: How many orbitals are present in any d subshell?
questions.explanation: l = 2 gives 2l + 1 = 5 d orbitals.

questions.stem: A nodal surface is where the electron probability is
questions.explanation: On a node ψ = 0, so |ψ|² = 0.

questions.stem: Relative to 1s, the 2s orbital has
questions.explanation: Radial nodes = n − l − 1 = 2 − 0 − 1 = 1 for 2s.

questions.stem: The number of radial nodes in an orbital is
questions.explanation: Radial (spherical) nodes equal n − l − 1.

questions.stem: Angular nodes in an orbital equal
questions.explanation: The number of angular nodes is the azimuthal quantum number l.

questions.stem: Total nodes of an orbital (radial + angular) equal
A 3p orbital has radial and angular nodes equal to
questions.explanation: Radial = 3 − 1 − 1 = 1; angular = l = 1.

questions.stem: For a 4d orbital the radial-node count is
In a 3d orbital you find
options: two radial nodes and no angular node
no radial node and two angular nodes
one radial and one angular node
questions.explanation: Radial = 3 − 2 − 1 = 0; angular = 2.

questions.stem: The Aufbau principle says electrons occupy
options: the lowest available energy orbitals first
questions.explanation: Orbitals are filled in order of increasing energy.

questions.stem: Pauli's exclusion rule forbids two electrons in an atom from having
questions.explanation: Each electron in an atom must have a unique (n, l, mₗ, mₛ) set.

questions.stem: When degenerate orbitals are available, Hund's rule prefers
options: maximum unpaired electrons with parallel spins
opposite spins in different subshells only
questions.explanation: Electrons occupy separate equal-energy orbitals singly and with parallel spins before pairing.

questions.stem: (n + l) rule is used to decide
options: the order of filling of orbitals
questions.explanation: The subshell with smaller n + l fills first; if tied, smaller n fills first.

questions.stem: In a neutral atom 4s is filled before 3d because
options: 4s has lower energy (smaller n + l) than 3d
questions.explanation: 4s has n + l = 4 while 3d has n + l = 5, so 4s lies lower for the isolated atom.

questions.stem: Between 3p and 4s, the orbital occupied earlier is
questions.explanation: Both have n + l = 4, but 3p has smaller n, so it fills first.

questions.stem: A single orbital can hold at most
questions.explanation: Pauli allows two electrons per orbital only if their spins are opposite.

questions.stem: Hund's rule applies to orbitals that are
questions.explanation: It governs filling of a set of equal-energy orbitals such as the three 2p orbitals.

questions.stem: Nitrogen's 2p³ configuration, by Hund, has unpaired electrons numbering
questions.explanation: Each of the three 2p orbitals gets one electron, all with parallel spins.

questions.stem: The filling sequence 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p continues with
questions.explanation: After 3p comes 4s, then 3d.

questions.stem: Extra stability of half-filled subshells is often invoked to explain
questions.explanation: Cr is 4s¹ 3d⁵ so that 3d is exactly half filled.

questions.stem: After 4s, the next subshell to fill in Aufbau order is
questions.explanation: The order is 4s, 3d, 4p.

questions.stem: For 5s and 4d the (n + l) values are respectively
questions.explanation: 5s: 5 + 0 = 5; 4d: 4 + 2 = 6, so 5s fills first.

questions.stem: Ground-state carbon (2p²) has how many unpaired electrons according to Hund?
questions.explanation: The two 2p electrons occupy different orbitals with parallel spins.

questions.stem: Oxygen (2p⁴) has unpaired electrons equal to
questions.explanation: Two 2p electrons pair in one orbital and the other two stay unpaired: ↑↓ ↑ ↑.

questions.stem: For carbon 2p², the Hund-violating arrangement is
options: two electrons in different 2p orbitals with parallel spins
both electrons paired in one 2p orbital with the others empty
questions.explanation: Pairing in one orbital while degenerate partners are vacant violates Hund's rule.

questions.stem: The correct Hund filling of 2p⁴ is
questions.explanation: Four 2p electrons: one orbital paired and two orbitals singly occupied.

questions.stem: 4p and 3d have n + l equal to 5; the one filled first is
questions.explanation: On an (n + l) tie the subshell with smaller n is filled first, so 3d before 4p.

questions.stem: Ground-state hydrogen is
questions.explanation: Hydrogen has a single electron in 1s.

questions.stem: Helium's ground configuration is
questions.explanation: Both electrons occupy 1s with opposite spins.

questions.stem: Carbon (Z = 6) has the ground configuration
questions.explanation: After 1s² 2s² the remaining two electrons enter 2p.

questions.stem: The ground configuration of nitrogen (Z = 7) is
questions.explanation: Seven electrons: 1s² 2s² 2p³ (half-filled 2p).

questions.stem: Oxygen (Z = 8) is represented in the ground state by
questions.explanation: Eight electrons give 1s² 2s² 2p⁴.

questions.stem: Neon (Z = 10) has the closed-shell configuration
questions.explanation: Neon completes the n = 2 shell: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶.

questions.stem: Sodium (Z = 11) is written as
questions.explanation: The extra electron beyond neon occupies 3s.

questions.stem: Chlorine (Z = 17) has the valence configuration
questions.explanation: Cl is [Ne] 3s² 3p⁵, one electron short of argon.

questions.stem: Potassium (Z = 19) places its last electron in
questions.explanation: After argon, 4s fills before 3d, so K is [Ar] 4s¹.

questions.stem: Calcium (Z = 20) has the condensed ground configuration
questions.explanation: Both extra electrons occupy 4s: [Ar] 4s².

questions.stem: Chromium (Z = 24) is an exception with configuration
questions.explanation: Cr is 4s¹ 3d⁵, giving a half-filled d set.

questions.stem: Copper (Z = 29) is correctly written as
questions.explanation: Cu is 4s¹ 3d¹⁰, a fully filled d subshell.

questions.stem: Iron (Z = 26) has the ground configuration
questions.explanation: Fe follows Aufbau as 4s² 3d⁶.

questions.stem: Manganese (Z = 25) is
questions.explanation: Mn is 4s² 3d⁵.

questions.stem: The ground configuration of zinc (Z = 30) is
questions.explanation: Zn completes 3d and 4s: [Ar] 4s² 3d¹⁰.

questions.stem: Fe²⁺ is formed from Fe by loss of two 4s electrons, leaving
questions.explanation: Transition-metal cations lose ns electrons first; Fe²⁺ is 3d⁶.

questions.stem: The cuprous ion Cu⁺ has the configuration
questions.explanation: Cu is 4s¹ 3d¹⁰; losing the 4s electron leaves 3d¹⁰.

questions.stem: Cr³⁺ has how many 3d electrons?
questions.explanation: Cr is 4s¹ 3d⁵; Cr³⁺ loses 4s¹ and two 3d electrons, leaving 3d³.

questions.stem: Chromium prefers 4s¹ 3d⁵ rather than 4s² 3d⁴ because
options: a half-filled 3d⁵ set is extra stable
3d is always filled before 4s in every atom
questions.explanation: Exchange energy / half-filled subshell stability favours 3d⁵ 4s¹.

questions.stem: Copper(II) ion Cu²⁺ has the d-electron count
questions.explanation: From 4s¹ 3d¹⁰, Cu²⁺ loses the 4s electron and one 3d electron, leaving 3d⁹.

questions.stem: A species is paramagnetic when it has
questions.explanation: Unpaired spins give a net magnetic moment and paramagnetism.

questions.stem: A diamagnetic atom or ion has
questions.explanation: Paired electrons cancel magnetic moments, producing diamagnetism.

questions.stem: Ground-state nitrogen atom is paramagnetic with unpaired electrons numbering
questions.explanation: 2p³ with Hund filling leaves three unpaired electrons.

questions.stem: Neon is diamagnetic because
options: its 2p subshell is completely filled and paired
questions.explanation: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ has no unpaired electron.
